title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 12: Republic v. Molina: Setting the Procedure for Nullifying a Marriage
keywords: most liberal divorce procedure in the world
root cause of the psychological incapacity
primary_topics: Chapter 12 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Republic v. Molina, the unanimous ponencia in which he refused to void the Molina marriage for psychological incapacity and, far more importantly, laid down eight procedural guidelines for every future Article 36 case.

The problem the case answered: since the Family Code's effectivity the courts had been swamped with Article 36 petitions, and the provision was 'used, abused and misused as a convenient "divorce law"' -- the OSG itself calling it the 'most liberal divorce procedure in the world.'

The substantive holding: psychological incapacity is confined to the most serious personality disorders showing 'utter insensitivity or inability to give meaning and significance to the marriage,' characterized by gravity, juridical antecedence and incurability, and existing at the celebration of the marriage -- not mere difficulty, neglect, refusal, irreconcilable differences or conflicting personalities.

CJP's defense of the decision against the charge of strictness, his view that the Supreme Court's function 'is to teach and to open new vistas,' and his record of the three Separate Opinions (Padilla, Romero, Vitug) that concurred in the result.
sub_topics: Article 36 of the Family Code introduced an entirely new ground for voiding a marriage, and the courts were thereafter swamped with petitions invoking it as a convenient divorce law rather than a ground for declaring a marriage inexistent from the beginning.

In its Petition the Office of the Solicitor General labeled Article 36 the 'most liberal divorce procedure in the world' and asked the Court not only to settle the Molina dispute but to issue procedural guidelines for the new remedy.

The facts: Roridel Olaviano Molina, married to Reynaldo on April 14, 1985 at San Agustin Church in Manila, alleged his immaturity and irresponsibility, his squandering of money on peers, his dependence on his parents and his eventual abandonment of her and their son Andre; Reynaldo blamed her friends, her refusal to cook and her handling of the household.
The RTC of La Trinidad, Benguet declared the marriage void and the Court of Appeals affirmed; the Republic, through the OSG, sought review in the Supreme Court.

The ruling: the marriage could not be voided, because what was shown was 'difficulty,' 'negligence' or 'refusal' rather than incapacity, and mere 'irreconcilable differences' and 'conflicting personalities' do not amount to psychological incapacity -- the parties must be shown incapable because of a psychological, not physical, illness.

CJP locates the real significance of the Decision not in the refusal to void the marriage but in the formulation of rules for evaluating similar cases, since 'the function of the Supreme Court is to teach and to open new vistas.'

Guidelines 1 to 4: the plaintiff bears the burden of proof and doubt is resolved in favor of the marriage, which the Constitution and the Family Code cherish as inviolable; the root cause must be medically or clinically identified, alleged, proven by experts and explained in the decision; the incapacity must exist at 'the time of the celebration'; and it must be medically or clinically permanent or incurable, though incurability may be relative to the other spouse only.

Guidelines 5 and 6: the illness must be grave enough to disable the party from assuming essential marital obligations -- 'mild characteriological peculiarities, mood changes, occasional emotional outbursts' will not do -- and those obligations are those in Articles 68 to 71 and Articles 220, 221 and 225 of the Family Code, which must be pleaded, proven and set out in the decision.

Guideline 7: interpretations of the National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal of the Catholic Church deserve great respect because Article 36 was taken from Canon 1095 of the 1983 Code of Canon Law, so that ideally what is canonically invalid should also be civilly void, the State and the Church walking 'together in synodal cadence' while remaining separate.

Guideline 8: the trial court must order the prosecuting attorney and the Solicitor General to appear for the state, and no decision may issue without the Solicitor General's certification of his agreement or opposition, filed within fifteen days -- a function equivalent to the defensor vinculi of Canon 1095.

CJP notes the ponencia was unanimously carried by the full 15-member Court, and answers the lawyers who call it strict: Molina 'is strict only insofar as Article 36 is construed as a divorce law,' but reasonable as a ground for declaring a marriage void -- one that never was, and so could not be 'cut.'

He records the three concurring Separate Opinions: Justice Padilla explaining his concurrence despite his dissent in Santos v. Court of Appeals; Justice Romero distinguishing incapacity from mental illness that would merely make a marriage annullable under Article 45, and recounting the Revision Committee's work and the Old Canon Law of 1917; and Justice Vitug reiterating the Santos tests he had penned.

stances.claim: Psychological incapacity under Article 36 reaches only the most serious personality disorders showing utter insensitivity or inability to give meaning to the marriage, and must be grave, juridically antecedent and incurable -- not mere difficulty, neglect, refusal or incompatibility.
stances.rhetorical_move: definitional narrowing, contrasting incapacity with difficulty, negligence and refusal

stances.claim: The real significance of the Decision lay not in refusing to void the Molina marriage but in issuing guidelines, because the function of the Supreme Court is to teach and to open new vistas.
stances.rhetorical_move: reframing the holding as a teaching act rather than a disposition of one dispute

stances.claim: Molina is strict only when Article 36 is read as a divorce law; read correctly, as a ground for declaring a marriage void from the beginning, it is reasonable -- a marriage that never was cannot be 'cut.'
stances.rhetorical_move: answering critics by relocating the disagreement to a premise about what Article 36 is

stances.claim: Canonical interpretations of the Church's matrimonial tribunal deserve great persuasive weight, since Article 36 was drawn from Canon 1095 to harmonize civil law with the religious faith of the people.
stances.rhetorical_move: source-and-purpose argument, pairing State and Church as walking 'in synodal cadence' while remaining separate

notable_anecdotes: CJP notes with evident satisfaction that his Molina ponencia was 'unanimously carried by the full 15-member Court,' an unusual show of agreement on a contested subject.

He reports the persistent criticism of Molina by 'many lawyers' for its alleged strictness, and gives his 'standard reply' -- that the decision is strict only if Article 36 is misread as a divorce law.

He recalls that the OSG itself, in its Petition, branded Article 36 the 'most liberal divorce procedure in the world' and asked the Court for guidelines, which is how the guidelines came to be written.
He recounts the three Separate Opinions, including Justice Padilla's explanation of why he concurred in Molina after dissenting in Santos v. Court of Appeals.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 12 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' recounted Republic v. Molina, the unanimous ponencia Artemio V. Panganiban wrote after Article 36 of the Family Code had swamped the courts with petitions and had been, in his words, used, abused and misused as a convenient divorce law -- the Office of the Solicitor General itself calling it the most liberal divorce procedure in the world and asking the Court for guidelines. Roridel Molina had won a declaration of nullity in the RTC of La Trinidad and in the Court of Appeals on the strength of her husband Reynaldo's immaturity, irresponsibility, squandering of money and eventual abandonment; the Republic sought review. The Court reversed, holding that psychological incapacity is confined to the most serious personality disorders indicating utter insensitivity or inability to give meaning and significance to the marriage, marked by gravity, juridical antecedence and incurability and existing when the marriage was celebrated. What Reynaldo showed was difficulty, negligence or refusal, and mere irreconcilable differences and conflicting personalities do not qualify. The real significance of the decision, CJP wrote, lay not in refusing to void the marriage but in the eight guidelines it issued, since the function of the Supreme Court is to teach and to open new vistas: the plaintiff bears the burden, with doubt resolved for the marriage the Constitution calls inviolable; the root cause must be medically identified, pleaded, proven by qualified psychiatrists or psychologists and explained in the decision; the incapacity must exist at the time of the celebration, be permanent or incurable, and be grave enough that mere characteriological peculiarities or emotional outbursts will not do; the obligations are those in Articles 68 to 71 and 220, 221 and 225; interpretations of the Church's National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal, given Article 36's origin in Canon 1095, deserve great respect; and the Solicitor General must certify his position as the equivalent of a defensor vinculi. Answering critics of the ruling's strictness, he replied that Molina is strict only insofar as Article 36 is construed as a divorce law, and he recorded the concurring Separate Opinions of Justices Padilla, Romero and Vitug.
